title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Repairing Qiskit Programs using Bugs4Q
authors: Saumya Brahmbhatt, Mitali Hukkeri, Dongchan Kim, M. V. Panduranga Rao, Lei Zhang
abstract: In quantum programs, Bugs4Q is a widely used benchmark containing real quantum defects. However, its evaluation assumes that benchmark labels remain valid and that generated fixes execute in the target environment. We evaluate two Bugs4Q versions containing 67 unique real Qiskit defects, adding executable tests where missing, and re-run all entries across six pinned Qiskit releases (0.25.0, 0.45.0, 1.0.0, 1.1.1, 2.0.0, and 2.3.1). We find that quantum benchmarks can suffer from silent label inversion: entries become invalid without errors when reference fixes stop executing or buggy programs no longer reproduce failures. Thus, correctness depends on the (benchmark, version) pair rather than the benchmark alone. We evaluate four LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5o-mini, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.4-mini), generating up to 10 repair candidates per defect and testing them across all versions. GPT-5.4 achieves the highest pass@10 (48.8%), followed by GPT-5.4-mini (47.3%), GPT-5o-mini (30.3%), and GPT-4o-mini (22.6%). All models perform best on Qiskit 0.45.0 and decline after the Qiskit 1.0 transition. Many failures arise from deprecated or incompatible APIs rather than incorrect repairs, and 64\% of successful repairs occur on entries invalid under the target version. We release a re-validated, version-pinned Bugs4Q benchmark and show that benchmark validation must precede repair evaluation.
summary: This paper evaluates how well large language models can fix bugs in quantum circuits written using Qiskit. The authors find that performance metrics are misleading because the underlying benchmark itself becomes invalid as the quantum framework updates. They conclude that robust evaluation requires explicitly pinning both the benchmark and the software version.
main_problem: The study benchmarks Large Language Models (LLMs) on automatically repairing quantum programs written in Qiskit using the Bugs4Q dataset.
main_result: LLM performance is highly dependent on the specific version of the underlying quantum framework (Qiskit), and many apparent successes are due to environmental compatibility rather than true repair correctness.
method: The authors evaluate four LLMs by generating multiple repair candidates for 67 known defects across six pinned versions of Qiskit, using pass@k metrics.
model_or_system: The system under test is quantum computation implemented via Qiskit programs containing real, documented defects sourced from the Bugs4Q benchmark.
key_observables: Pass@10 rate, executability status across different Qiskit versions, and the proportion of successful repairs occurring on invalid benchmark entries.
important_parameters: Six pinned Qiskit releases (e.g., 0.25.0 to 2.3.1), and the number of repair candidates tested per defect (up to 10).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption challenged is that benchmark labels remain valid across software updates; correctness depends on the (benchmark, version) pair.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the pass@10 rate peaking at Qiskit 0.45.0 and declining sharply after the Qiskit 1.0 transition, while Table III shows performance restricted to valid pairs.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of benchmarking quantum code repair, details the version-pinned evaluation protocol using Bugs4Q across multiple LLMs, presents results showing version dependency, and concludes by advocating for mandatory benchmark validation before repair assessment.
why_interesting: It establishes rigorous standards for evaluating AI assistance in quantum software development, which is crucial for any field relying on complex quantum circuit implementation.
